rejected.title: Terra nullius
card: Terra nullius is Latin for land belonging to no one. Historians use it to describe how Britain treated Australia, though the term itself came into use later.
Britain took possession as if no one owned the land. It made no treaty with the First Nations peoples whose Country it was, and did not buy land from them.
Yet First Nations peoples had lived on and cared for the land for tens of thousands of years, under their own laws.
In the Mabo case in 1992, the High Court rejected terra nullius. It found that First Nations peoples' rights to land had existed before Britain arrived, and could still exist.
rejected.remember: Britain acted as if the land had no owners, and the High Court rejected that idea in 1992.

a.q: Why did the High Court reject terra nullius in the Mabo case?
opts: Land rights existed before Britain arrived
Britain had signed a treaty for the land
No one had lived on the land before 1788
Britain had paid the owners for the land
a.why: The High Court found that First Nations peoples had rights to land before Britain arrived, so the land had not belonged to no one. Britain made no treaty and bought no land, so those options are wrong.
a.clue: Did the land have owners before 1788?

b.q: Why did Britain make no treaty with First Nations peoples when it took possession of Australia?
opts: It treated the land as if it had no owners
It had already bought the land from them
The High Court told it not to make one
It had agreed to share the land with them
b.why: Britain acted as if the land belonged to no one, so it saw no owners to make a treaty with. It did not buy the land or agree to share it, and the High Court ruling came much later, in 1992.
b.clue: Think about who Britain saw as the owners.

version.title: Terra nullius
card: Terra nullius is Latin for land belonging to no one. The term came into use later, to name the way Britain treated Australia.
From 1788 Britain claimed the land as if it had no owners. It made no treaty, a formal agreement, with the First Nations peoples whose Country it was, and did not buy land from them.
Yet First Nations peoples had owned and cared for their Country for tens of thousands of years, under their own laws.
In the Mabo case in 1992, the High Court rejected terra nullius. It found that First Nations peoples' rights to land had existed before 1788, and could still exist.
version.remember: Britain acted as if the land had no owners, and in 1992 the High Court said that was wrong.

a.q: Why is the idea of terra nullius false for Australia?
opts: First Nations peoples owned the land under their laws
Britain signed a treaty with every First Nations people
The land was empty until the First Fleet arrived
The High Court found Britain had paid for the land
a.why: Terra nullius means land belonging to no one, but First Nations peoples had owned and cared for their Country for tens of thousands of years under their own laws. Britain made no treaty and bought no land, so those options are wrong.
a.clue: Who was living on the land in 1788?

b.q: Britain signed a treaty with Māori chiefs in New Zealand in 1840, but made none in Australia. Which idea helps explain why?
opts: Britain treated the land as having no owners
First Nations peoples sold the land to Britain
The High Court banned treaties in Australia
Britain made a treaty that was later lost
b.why: Britain acted as if the land in Australia belonged to no one, an idea later called terra nullius, so it saw no owners to make a treaty with. First Nations peoples did not sell the land: Britain made no treaty and bought no land.
b.clue: Who did Britain think owned the land?

a.best: First Nations peoples owned the land under their laws

b.best: Britain treated the land as having no owners
